note.note: In early modern plays, the stage direction thunder and lightning was very common, and the effects of thunder and lightning produced in a variety of different ways. In this play, it’s assumed that the stage direction thunder and lightning is directly linked to a storm (Dessen and Thomson, 231). Making the sounds of thunder and lightning could have been achieved through drums, flashes of fire, and fireworks. This type of effect was created in the tiring house. They were noted by the bookkeeper in the manuscript playbook used backstage so that he could cue for the effect at the right time (Thomson, 14). In many other plays, the effects of thunder and lightning were linked to the supernatural, and accompanied figures such as devils and witches, who might ascend from a trapdoor that signified the underworld. An audience would expect something supernatural when this particular effect occured (Thomson, 11).

It’s important to remember that a performer in early modern plays could have expected to perform in a venue that was a rectangular, flat, largely empty stage [with] no sets in the modern sense (Syme, 112). Thus, we can assume that there was not actually a physical ship on stage. Therefore, in order to portray some sort of sea voyage, the use of ropes, tackle boxes, and other sailing equipment could have aided the impression of being at sea, with characters pulling on cords found in the tiring house. The stage was seen as the deck, the tiring house as the cabin of the ship, and the balcony as the mast or the lookout area. During this play, it’s also clear that the characters on the boat are fighting against strong waves; this illusion could have been made by the characters acting wild and hysterical (McInnis, 118).
float or drift with wind or current

The special effects used during live performances in early modern England would depend heavily on the budget of the playhouse; they could range from austere and simple to grand and elaborate (Syme, 112-14). Different effects such as drums, the firing of canons, and even fireworks could have been used to give the illusion that the actors and audience were actually in the center of a raging tempest.
a ship’s officer in charge of equipment
an exclamation calling for attention or to cease
The implication is that fish wait for her in the ocean, or perhaps under decks (Bourne).

The sweet sin breeders the shipmaster is referring to are women (here, specifically, Aminta, as she is the only woman on the boat). The shipmaster believes that everyone on the ship is going to die because they won’t have any help from the heavens, and he blames this entirely on Aminta. Many times, women were denied passage on ships; if they happened to be on board, they were either a captive, a slave, or being forced to marry (Moore, 318). In Aminta’s next speech below, it becomes clear that she has been captured by Albert, and that he has forced her to be on his ship for his own pleasure. Ironically, Aminta is only on the ship because of him, yet she is still being blamed for compromising the ability of the men to control the boat during the dangerous storm.
i.e. a more fully felt or accumulated

In the 1647 text of the play, question marks are used to punctuate Oh … redeem me and How … ye, but sometimes, in the seventeenth century, compositors would use question marks where we would use exclamation points today (Jackson, 549). Thus, the lines (as presented here) illustrate Aminta’s raging anger and hatred for Albert if the question marks are meant to be interpreted as exclamation points. Question marks in this scene give off a completely different meaning: they would account for Aminta’s confusion as to whether she should curse and hate Albert. Regardless, one cannot be sure as to when Aminta exactly falls in love with Albert, but it’s crucial to consider that she is his prisoner before their love blossoms.
raked, i.e. accumulated; possibly also wrecked

On board this ship, there is a very interesting mix of characters from various social classes. Three of the men—Lamure, Franville, and Morillat—are French lords. In the early modern period, clothing helped establish a person’s identity and located their position in a variety of categories ranging from gender, class, nationality, and religion (Lublin, 10). Thus, when Lamure’s clothes and goods are thrown overboard, his response is that he feels completely ruined and destroyed (i.e. undone). Although this may seem dramatic to the modern reader, these characters experience a loss of material goods as a loss of identity. Furthermore, because Lamure is a self-made man (lines 137-140), he loses the noble identity he has created for himself (apparently by dubious means) and now fears being seen as equal to those of a lower class that he spent twenty years trying to buy his way out of.
British coins with a value of five shillings

Among Tibalt’s listed possessions are false dice, which are trick or weighted dice. Used as a prop, they are a physical manifestation for the actor to demonstrate the kind of wayward person that Tibalt is. And if the dice are not shown on stage and are instead just mentioned by name only, then it grants a quick snapshot of someone who values a handful of cheat dice as some of the things he keeps with him when he has so few possessions: skin, clothes, sword, self, two crowns, two pair of cards, and three false dice (lines 162-165). His possessions portray him as a kind of traveling vagabond, a drifter that goes town to town and makes a living by gambling and violence.
term of address often used in consideration of bravery
Fortune was often depicted as veiled
i.e. What flag does their ship fly?
comforting or reviving medicine or beverage

[T]here might be accompanied by a gesture towards the audience. The architecture of the outdoor playhouses, with standing-room around the stage, meant that actors could gesture or look to the audience to create a sense of the imagined space of the sea or anything that is being referred to at a distance (Syme, 95).
suffer from overindulgence in food or drink
tube used to insert medicine into the rectum
music to accompany a quick and lively dance; also, the dance itself
fine, crisp fabric of a plain weave
Roman goddess of beauty and love
suits of clothing; also, a reference to the skin as the body’s suit

Tibalt tries to defend Albert and the Captain’s orders to discard the men’s belongings for the safety of the crew. He challenges Franville by saying there is no one here to admire his suits, i.e. there are no people to impress with the fabrics they are made up of or how he looks while wearing them. Additionally, there is also no one there to buy his suits (i.e. to turn them into metal, or coins). According to Tibalt, Franville’s most important suit is his own body, specifically his skin.
close-fitting jackets worn primarily by men
light sword that can be used in one hand
British coins with a value of five shillings

Tibalt’s monologue acts as a social commentary and revolves around how much importance noblemen gave to their material possessions, to the point where they evaluated their virtues and characters based on material goods. He begins by urging them to be grateful for having skin that is not corrupted by venereal disease (purled with scabs/ancient monuments to Madam Venus). Their skin, he continues, will never go out of fashion or abandon them until their bodies decayed after death and were devoured by worms. The purpose of this monologue is to acquaint the audience (and readers) with how social hierarchy was determined by material possessions by having Tibalt satirize the social practice. He suggests that having clothes represent our accomplishments as individuals is just as ridiculous as fish appearing in the clothes that have now sunk to the bottom of the sea.
And some friends I can make
i.e. I can bring the others to my side
Surgical cupping glass, or possibly lidded case for ointments
feelings of pity, devotion, and faithfulness
i.e. a more fully felt or accumulated plague
i.e. one who feeds off money and material possessions
finely, splendidly; also, characteristic of behavior appropriate to noble status

Sebastian does not go into detail about how long he and Nicusa have been stranded on the island. Descriptions of their physical state and appearance, such as goodly long manes and sunk eyes, provide some clues, but these details are not enough to indicate an exact number of years. The unspecified number of years opens up interpretation not only to how long the men have been stranded, but how long they have been separated from the Portuguese women. We later learn that enough time has passed for Clarinda, who seems to have come to the island as a very small child, to grow to sexual maturity.
from Greek mythology, referring to the threads of fate
i.e. make more fully felt or accumulated
i.e. not able to cross the river
figuratively tilling fields, more generally a means of earning one’s livelihood
those who apportion or carve meat at the table
contemptuous address used to men and boys

A reference to two of the five different ages of man from Greek mythology; the Golden Age was the first and best age. Iron refers to the last and worst age of mankind, signaling the transition of Albert’s crew from a state of comfort and civility to a state of brutishness and toil. Also a reference to Tibalt’s sword.
valuable goods, i.e. Sebastian and Nicusa’s gold
those who apportion or carve meat at the table
apportion or carve meat at the table; here also referring to attacking with a sword
leg or haunch of an animal
healing ointments for wounds or sores
referring to herb-of-grace, another name for common rue
What a veal voice is there
Tibalt is comparing the question of the crew members to the bawling of calves
one who provides lodgings; a host
i.e. strong halters for hanging and providing quick death (Bourne)
the open air; also, a reference to the English court established in the 15th century to try socially and politically important defendants
festers, esp. to a degree that causes pain
This moment depicts a sacrifice of body for body with clear religious connotations playing on the word altar (as she alters her own body to save his).
from Greek mythology, referring to a river in Hades that causes forgetfulness

This phrasing suggests Albert blames Nature (here, personified) for putting him and Aminta into this harsh environment. To bolster his point, he provides two examples of Nature’s unfair treatment of them: the first one is that nature gives a drunkard more wine, and a glutton more food, though the drunkard has already drunk and has no need for more wine, and the glutton already has enough food. Thus, Albert attempts to shame Nature into providing aid to her more deserving victims, especially Aminta (a virgin who is pin[ing] for hunger).

Albert hears music from the neighboring island. We eventually learn that the makers of this music are Portuguese women, which means that the music heard here might have had influences from Portugal, and possibly its colonies in the Middle East and West India. A major context for the play is European colonial dominion over other parts of the world, indicated in part by how it mimics Shakespeare’s The Tempest. It is possible that some of the common music instruments possessed by the Portuguese (or instruments imagined by the playwrights to be possessed by them) could have been showcased or approximated on stage. In addition to horns, another possible sound that might have been recreated on stage is of the adufe, a square double-skinned frame drum traditionally played by women on the Iberian Peninsula. The skins are sewn together, often with seeds between them; it is held with the thumbs of both hands and the pointer of the right hand, leaving the other fingers free to hit the instrument. This instrument was introduced into Portugal (and Spain) when the Moors of North Africa conquered the Iberian Peninsula in the 8th century. (Schecter)
Greek god of the west wind
risks of loss or harm, dangers
characterized by exciting pleasure or ecstasy
one bound or devoted to worship or a particular vow
political body in which every member has a voice or vested interest

As the commonwealth’s rules forbid any contact with men (thus ruling out any forms of reproduction), these same rules will lead to the ultimate demise of the women and, with them, the commonwealth itself.
Roman goddess of beauty and love
Roman goddess of hunting and virginity
non-Christian, thought also at this time to be uncivilized

rules, laws, or decrees, usually ecclesiastical. This word choice goes hand-in-hand with the ongoing theme of faith and religion throughout this play. Disobeying the canons not only breaks the commonwealth law but is also figured here as a type of sin.
exclamation inciting shame, usually said to children
from Greek mythology, referring to the river Styx which divided Earth from the underworld
from Greek mythology, referring to Elysium, the heavenly paradise for fallen Greek heroes
i.e. if you are not goddesses
i.e. Diana, Roman goddess of hunting and virginity
The combined effect of the references to Elysium, Styx, and Diana show a shift from Albert’s presumably French Catholic faith to a classical mythological frame of mind.
acknowledge or bestow in some favorable manner
i.e. Aminta’s beauty approaches that of the commonwealth women
Crocale is referring to the command from Rosella that all commonwealth women refuse men’s company.
i.e. Diana, Roman goddess of hunting and virginity
medicines containing a single active ingredient, derived directly from nature without human manipulation

Though the phrase Arabian groves is vague, it could suggest the increased cross-pollination of horticulture between Europe and the Middle East and India. Portugal had colonized several territories (Bahrain, Sohar, Julfar, Quriyat), now constituting modern-day Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, during the reign of the Iberian Union between 1580-1640 (de Oliveira Marques, 322). The Amazons are also believed to have originated in Libya and to have migrated across Syria, Egypt, Scythia (Foreman). The Arabian groves reference could refer to the coconut and palm trees that were commonly seen on the coast of Southwest India. After the conquests of Vasco Da Gama, Portugal colonized territories like Bombay and Goa by the Arabian Sea before India’s major colonization by the British in the late seventeenth century (Narayanan, 198). It is therefore possible for Indian horticultural features to appear in an imagined Portuguese aesthetic.

Perhaps a reference to the chameleon’s ability to blend into its surroundings, i.e. Clarinda will need to render her desire for Albert invisible because of the commonwealth’s law against interacting with men. More likely, though, this refers to the belief that chameleons survived solely on air since Clarinda has been referring to Albert’s breath. See William Shakespeare’s The Two Gentlemen of Verona, where chameleons are referenced as both air-eaters and color-changers.
i.e. Kind acts are their own reward and do not require praise
i.e. Though Clarinda has never met a man, instinctually she knows about sexual attraction.

Rosella likens Albert to the figure of the siren to reinforce her argument that men are dangerously manipulative. Based in Greek mythology, sirens were creatures that were part-women, part-bird or mermaid. They would lure sailors to destruction by enchanting them with song. Sirens have been traditionally gendered as women, but Rosella inverts this association, emphasizing Albert’s manipulation. This linguistic inversion points to the larger theme of reversing traditional gender roles within play.
in this case, maintain, adhere to
support, often in a spiritual or ecclesiastical sense
i.e. Can this single man provide all the commonwealth women with children
born into nobility; also, of gentle manners

Rosella’s command is that any boys born by the commonwealth women will be given to the men, while any girls will stay with the women and become part of the commonwealth. The historical Amazons were supposedly neighbors to an all-male society called the Gargareans. They met annually for a mating ritual. The female children born after this ritual were retained by the Amazons, and the male children went to their fathers (Strabo). Rosella’s reference to this practice of mating with an all-male society had historical precedent. It also provides some geographical hints. As the Gargareans and Amazons are believed to have reigned between Eurasia and the Middle East, the play hints at taking place in the Mediterranean or Black Sea. (Indeed, the play references a black river between the barren and fertile islands.)
natural dwellings, habitations, or abodes typically used for amorous meetings

The long dash closing this act (present in the 1647 folio text) adds a level of ambiguity to the exit. Other instances of long dashes in the 1647 folio are used to indicate interruptions in the dialogue. Therefore, we could assume that Albert is being interrupted at the closing of the scene, though the text does not give indication of exactly what or who could be interrupting Albert. The long dash could allow actors to vary the portrayal of this end scene. One implication could be that Albert and Clarinda walk out of the stage with redundant pleasantries, formalities, and exchanges that the authors and printers did not deem worthy of consuming the page’s highly sought-for space. Another implication could be that the next scene immediately follows as they exit. The dash could also represent space on the page, indicating that more words were spoken here, up to the actors’ or the company’s discretion or improvisation.

A possible version of the idiom: one man’s poison is another man’s meat, essentially meaning people have different tastes or value is relative. The idiom was used by Beaumont and Fletcher’s contemporary Thomas Middleton in his 1604 work Plato’s Cap (That old moth-eaten proverb… One man’s meat, is another man’s poison), though also by Beaumont himself in Love’s Cure, which was also published for the first time in the 1647 folio: What’s one man’s poison, Signor, is another’s meat or drink. In a literal way, the palates of the shipwrecked nobles must shift from meat to mud (poison). At the same time, it may suggest that societal rules/morality are also relative: one man’s good behavior (meat) is another one’s bad (poison) and vice versa. But in the context of the shipwreck, poison suggests a kind of moral suspension: the behavior that was once deemed bad in society is no longer considered bad on the island.
close-fitting jacket worn primarily by men
portion of meat from an adult sheep, often considered less palatable than other meats
surgical cupping glasses, or possibly lidded cases for ointments
soft materials used for dressing wounds
medicinal pieces of cloths used on wounds
rolls of soft, absorbent material, which were often medicated and used to stop wounds from bleeding
medicine administered through a bodily orifice, usually the rectum
comforting or reviving medicine or beverage
prepared bladder of an animal, inflated and used as a receptacle for substances like medicine
plant-based medicine used for soothing fevers
substance applied to the skin as part of a bandage
wart, cyst, tumor, or other protuberance of the body
collection of goods, in this case, food
healing ointment for wounds or sores
a foolish person, or a vain man

Discourse on cannibalism in the early modern period became more prevalent following European contact with real and imagined cannibals in North and South America. Cannibalism in the Americas was largely reviled by Europeans. However, during the period this play was written there was also a medicinal cannibalistic practices thriving throughout Europe. The medicinal discourse between Lamure, Morillat, Franville, and the Surgeon earlier in the play are relevant to this discussion in that they consider eating a wen that was pulled from one of the sailor’s shoulders during the voyage. Prior to this, the group primarily discusses tools of medicine; the brief mention of cordials, potions, and pills takes on a different meaning due to many medications being made from human parts, with some of the most common sources being blood and bone (Sugg).
possessions, goods, often with relation to livestock

In pre-modern physiology, the humors were four different fluids in the body; when imbalanced, one’s body and mood risked falling out of health and displaying the symptoms related to the type of imbalance. The word humorous is also used to mean moody or capricious. Being a doctor (and thus knowledgeable of the humors), the Surgeon wishes to remove them from Aminta’s body before the men eat her. Yet the act of removing her humors is telling. In one way, he expresses concern for his health by emptying the humors: if he were to eat Aminta’s humors, he could contract an imbalance—whether an excess or a deficit—of his own humors. At the same time, Aminta is female and so stereotyped in early modern drama as capricious and changeable. This could suggest the Surgeon fears he could contract her emotionality over his balanced male rationality if he were to eat her. This line could also be read, more simply, as an indication of the Surgeon’s desire to eat the humorous (i.e. juicy) parts of her body.
expression of surprise used to emphasize what follows
expression of surprise used to emphasize what follows
i.e. Aminta may produce children which will serve as further food
fleshy or muscular parts of the body
choke with a mouthful of food
ferocious dogs chained or tied up to guard a house
serve; presumably a threat of violence

martyred third-century French saint who is said to have carried his head for several miles after he was beheaded. Tibalt implies the sailors only attend to their bodily needs and desires (Bourne)

referring to the Christian time of abstinence and repentance
buy medicines thought to enhance sexual performance

ambitious rivalry for power or honor
Roman goddess of beauty and love, here referring also to the planet

As Tibalt explains how he selected a partner for Albert, he refers to astrology, saying that Albert was born under Saturn, a malignant planet, which caused him to be prone to melancholy. In the early modern period, the medical belief in the humoral system still persisted. This meant that there were four bodily humors: phlegm, yellow bile, blood, and black bile, that could cause various issues if these fluids were unbalanced. Melancholy was the term for an excess of black bile. The humoral system often was used in conjunction with theories about the planets (namely, the moon, Mars, Venus, Jupiter, and Saturn). In this case, Tibalt selects Clarinda because he claims that she is a soft, ruddy wench born under Venus. This, according to Tibalt should restore Albert’s balance and counteract his melancholic tendencies. Melancholy was also blamed for hallucinations, sudden outbursts, and other signs of madness.
ready to ride, used as sexual innuendo
fictional female warrior and expert in combat
the part of a Muslim palace where wives and concubines live
sweet drinks made with syrup or sugar
drug prepared from the resin of a tree of the West Indies
plums; also, liqueurs derived from the fruit of the blackthorn
a bitter pharmaceutical substance used as an antaphrodisiac

i.e. I do not often engage in sexual activity
i.e. rich widows expect large sums of money as gifts

an individual who is skilled in the work surrounding gems and precious stones

The phrase idol of lapidary begins a series of descriptions of the treasure by the Frenchmen that seemingly elevates its value to a mythical quality through associations with a diverse variety of individuals—slaves, merchants, royalty, sailors—who would go to immense lengths to possess it. Idol of lapidary also implies that the treasure is a divine object of worship, perhaps even beyond one’s love of God. While these descriptions aim to impress Rosella, in a larger sense they function to afford the men themselves material value alongside their sexual value to the women. It is therefore of utmost importance to the Frenchmen to upsell the value of the treasure. Furthermore, in a narrative with characters like Lamure, Franville, and Morillat, whose identities are strongly rooted in their material wealth (as first seen in Act 1, Scene 1 during the storm), perhaps these people-related descriptions of value mirror their own views on persona and reflect a genuine desire for such treasure to re-establish their identities.

Rosella’s call of gratitude to the stars for bringing her an opportunity for revenge subtly contrasts Albert’s earlier pleas to a Christian heaven. While both reference some type of higher force intertwined with the Christian beliefs of the time, Rosella references a naturalistic force that, in a larger sense, emphasizes the women’s eschewing of societal and religious conventions in their isolated environment. The women are previously characterized alongside the Greek goddess Artemis as independent, chaste hunters and with Artemis’ associations with the moon. Here, the women appeal to a Greek, polytheistic religion that places belief in the power of celestial bodies like the moon and the stars. This association also perhaps alludes to the idea of women constantly changing and being influenced by nature. Taken together with the men’s references to conventional Christian ideas of God and heaven, a rhetorical battle is created not only between spiritual worldviews, but also between genders.
i.e. Part of what was presented to me by the French men

The original definition of jointure is rooted in marriage conventions, referring to an arrangement between a husband and wife to hold a property jointly so that the property may be settled on the wife if she is widowed. It also has been used an equivalent term to a dowry. Tibalt’s use of jointures, then, might allude to the societal and patriarchal need to establish order through marital and legal conventions, particularly as this usage occurs in the face of a woman’s (Rosella’s) anger. However, the suggested convention of jointure is one of the few of its time that gave women potential independence over their estate, and so it may also be rhetorically appropriate that Tibalt offers a share of further wealth to Rosella who is presumed to be widowed (Habakkuk, 15). It is also possible that jointure’s associations with dowry suggest that an intense situation of environment isolated from societal norms could lead to a switch in gender roles, such as a man freely offering dowry directly to a woman.
very small offering of something, in this case, nourishment
path travelled by person or animal

Using the term gallants to describe the men that Sebastian and Nicusa reported being on the island is significant because it indicates Raymond’s class expectations. Gallants is a term that describes young men as smartly or” finely-dressed” who are gorgeous or showy in appearance. In a way, Raymond is reminding Sebastian and Nicusa that they had described a group of men on the island who were well-dressed, which would mean they are of the higher or wealthier class. Ironically, gallants is a term that is very much the opposite of what one would expect to find on the barren island where, as the audience knows by this point, there is no chance of prosperity. Because these men are so contrasting to what the island looks like and could support, it stands to reason that it should also be doubly easy to find them.

divine guidance. The term marks another instance where a word’s non-religious and religious definitions can both function simultaneously. Sebastian could be stating that he does not know what foresight and/or supplies may have allowed the Frenchmen to guide themselves away from the island, but he could also be suggesting that some sort of divine protection and guidance may have played a part in the men not being present. This call for the involvement of or help from a higher force is the first of many from Sebastian, as he and Nicusa are accused further of making false claims, participating in the absence of the men, and finally acting unlike Christian gentleman.
clear from accusation or suspicion; also, to vomit
persons of common or low status and rank with connotations of dishonesty and cunningness
ironic name for the desolate island
path travelled by person or animal
Rosella refers to the coming anniversary of her and Sebastian’s wedding
i.e. most fully felt or executed

Fletcher and Massinger give us a play that can easily be read as a commentary on the greed driving European colonization. Rosella’s criticism of the French stems from her view of their actions as an attempt to control their commonwealth by robbing valuable things from them. As Rita Banerjee notes, The critique of piracy in The Sea Voyage centers especially on the inordinate desire for gold and treasure (294). At the start of the scene, Rosella echoes Tibalt’s sentiment from the beginning of the play when he tells the other men to resist obsession with riches to preserve their lives. Because she holds the men responsible for stealing her husband’s treasure, Rosella intends to kill them as revenge, thus validating Tibalt’s prior warning and reinforcing the critique present throughout the play that riches mean nothing in the face of death; a focus on lust for gold and treasure in the play helps point out that the equating of material goods to personal worth and identity is dangerous and destructive. Of course, in the play’s backstory, the Portuguese women (and men) were, themselves, colonists at the time they were driven from their plantation by the French. With no mention of the native peoples who were presumably pillaged and displaced by their colonial project, the play elides the violence characteristic of European colonial settlement and figures the Portuguese squarely as victims.

i.e. they appear as dogs or persons of mixed or uncertain descent. The word mongrel is chiefly used in a derogatory manner, meaning that this mixed breeding is indicative of a lower form of life. This usage implies the importance of purity of nationality or race and points to an underlying conflict between the French and Portuguese throughout the play. It is also important to note that Juletta calls the Frenchmen gentlemen, but immediately rescinds that judgement when discussing their behavior. This juxtaposition of superficial appearance with demonstrated behavior also denotes a key conflict throughout the play.

Juletta’s speech here highlights a key contention throughout the play: the control of physical sustenance and that of reproductive success, both of which sustain life. Juletta is responsible for looking after her group of men: she is the one giving food to them, as well as presumably exercising sexual dominance over them, as suggested by her phrasing here. The way in which hunger, thirst, and sexual desire are regulated contrasts norms that denied women of the time a good deal of agency; the women in this play, however, are the ones in charge of all physical and sexual sustenance. Though this power is given to the Amazons and reflects an agency not typically experienced by women, their drive to reproduce was is still consistent with traditional pressures on women. As Claire Jowitt puts it, [T]he text draws a distinction between resources needed for immediate survival—food and water—and those necessary for medium and long-term colonization—children to be new generations of settlers (99). Though the women have a level of dominance as the food source for their prisoners and the survival source for their population, the burden of having such power is always evident. It is a burden which certainly arose within royal families when the queen was required to produce an heir. This would have been known to a seventeenth-century audience living under a monarchy. Both reproductive capacity and possession of property provide authority in the play, yet both also produce a certain level of balance. Possession and freedom are intertwined in the play—possession of riches and land enables possession of other people. The treasure initially belonged to the Amazons, giving them power, which is then supplemented by taking the men as their prisoners. But, eventually the power transfers back to the men when a concord is reached by marriage.
physically healthy; also, morally or intellectually healthy
exclamation inciting shame usually said to children
endurance of ongoing pain or penalty
i.e. be flexible, even against Rosella’s orders
I think that is your meaning

Clarinda’s promise of wealth and jewels to Albert in her hopes of wooing him acts as a dowry. In offering it, she also offers salvation as she plans to spare his life, thus enabling a future for life on the island itself through reproduction. She is actually reversing the original cause of enmity between the two groups by giving the stolen treasure back to him while hoping to attain their union, which, though she is unable to do without patriarchal sanction, represents the play’s harmonious ending by marriage between groups. As Jowitt notes, The plot of The Sea Voyage follows the haphazard and hostile interaction between these colonies until, finally, an understanding between the groups is achieved which enables them to pool resources(Jowitt, 99).

Although Aminta and Clarinda have come from different groups, they work together to sustain Albert. Clarinda’s nutritional provision for Albert is supplemented by Aminta’s romantic/sexual provision for him, which in turn makes possible the ensuing sequence of events that ends the play in a way that ensures the survival of all involved. The idea of union between two factions is again emphasized, but beyond that it juxtaposes the threat to survival posed by division and distinction between groups, neither of which have all the necessary means of survival without the other. As Jowitt points out, it is only between the separate factions [that] there are enough resources to ensure a sustainable lifestyle (99).

Based on the structure of many early modern playhouses, including the second Globe where this play was performed in 1622, it is likely the curtain to which Aminta refers is the arras across a discovery space in the middle of the tiring house wall which would have hidden Albert from view. As Syme notes, Even if there was no central stage door, there would have been an area between the two entrances that lay concealed behind an arras or curtain that could be drawn to reveal preset tableaux (115).

Bottarga (potargo) are dried and salted sacs of fish eggs, usually made from mullet or tuna. It is difficult and time-consuming to make because it involves salt baths, massaging, and weeks of aging. The Master’s joke here is doubly felt because the prisoners have no access to food at all, let alone a type of food that was difficult to make and considered a luxury. Bottarga is enjoyed more widely today, but it is still considered a delicacy (Squadrilli).
rope made of dried eel skin used for flogging, here used as a phallic image
one who frequently seeks out the company of women, with implications of promiscuity
exclamation inciting shame, usually said to children

This line has sexual connotations because in this era oysters were viewed as a venereal symbol and considered an aphrodisiac. More specifically, oysters were associated with vulvas. Beyond that, Gordon Williams notes that during the period a woman could be defined through her sexual part (982). The Master is essentially sexualizing the women and reducing them to their anatomy. Gape is additionally suggestive in this context as it could imply the Master and Tibalt resent the women’s power over their own sexuality: the women are imagined to be opening their own sexual anatomy and thus exerting control of their sexual fates.

Throughout this scene, identifying innuendo is imperative to understanding the exchange among the characters. In response to Crocale, who says Tibalt and the Master are not men, the Master assures her she will find a salt eel (a phallic symbol) if she should search them. This image is soon met by an observation that the women gape like oysters. As oysters were understood to represent the vagina, their gaping suggests the sexual desire of the women themselves. The phrase crept into us makes the sexual connotations of his speech unmistakable, allowing the necessities and wants of the women to equivocate with both sexual desire and the desire of obedience from the men. Sex is then tied to power for the women as it is to food for the men.
such a sordid impudence I’ll spit at

Much of Tibalt and the Master’s frustration with their imprisonment seems to be that they regard the women’s behavior as unwomanly. Tibalt is willing to accept a painful death, but he refuses to accept the commanding behavior and attitude of the women in charge of him, and states that he would be willing to accept their position if they acted more ladylike and milder. Tibalt and the Master seem to have strong perceptions of how women should act, and these Amazon women do not adhere to their expectations, suggesting it is the reversal of gender roles that is key to the conflict in this moment.

persons of common or low status and rank with connotations of dishonesty and cunningness
i.e. those who founder (or, drown) us

The French gentlemen, who boarded their ship as noblemen, describe themselves as almost nothing —rogues and knaves— and plead with Clarinda to put them in any service to live, even if it’s simply to help procreate. This exchange, and also the lines later when Morillat tells Clarinda to beat them if they offend them(which is an open admittance of their subservient positions at this time), speak to gender roles and the challenge that this play introduces to gender stereotypes. These men are now shipwrecked on an island where women are in charge and to which the men have brought almost no value; their own value, now, is procreative. In an era where men traditionally provide for the household but women ultimately create life, the power dynamic has been turned upside down, with both parties still depending on the other, but for reversed services.

In many instances in this play, meat also references a man’s sexual desire for a woman’s body. In The Sexual Politics of Meat, Carol Adams discusses the ways that references to meat-eating is directly linked to masculine aspects of our own modern culture (1). The Sea Voyage reflects this same dynamic throughout. For example, Morillat suggests that Albert captured Aminta for his own appetite. Throughout it is only the men who beg for meat and seem to have this kind of appetite. This emphasis on meat throughout, as opposed to other food sources, suggests that the The Sea Voyage is exploring the complicated ways in which meat and women’s bodies are equated during the early modern period.

In early modern drama, a table itself as a prop could be considered an extravagant display considering set design tended to be minimalistic. Money spent by theater companies was invested more in costumes than sets. As a result, plays during the period had remarkably spare stages, requiring the audience to rely heavily on their imagination to furnish the setting. Seeing a table furnished with lots of props would likely stand out to the audience, and suggests that the table will be the center of gravity for the scene. In other words, the action will revolve around the table, directly and indirectly.

In the original text, no stage directions are provided to indicate Crocale is hiding or has stepped aside. Additionally, no stage directions specify that Hippolita and Juletta exit. Rather, these actions must simply be inferred from the dialogue. During this period, performances accomplished hiding characters in several ways. In the Blackfriars Theatre, for example, Crocale could ’hide’ by sitting with the audience, as some of the audience in the Blackfriars sat on the side of the stage. Another place for Crocale to hide could be up on a balcony (which many early modern theaters had), watching the action from up above. The most important aspect of this stage direction is possibly not that Crocale is visible to the audience, but that the audience actually knows she is hiding.

These two ships and what was on each is yet another instance in this play where gender roles are challenged. The treasures and other valuable belongings of the travelers were all aboard the men’s ship, perhaps because these valuables would have been kept safe by them. Ironically, this proved to be quite the opposite; whereas the men landed on a desolate island, their crew eventually killing one another over the treasure, the women landed on the fertile island, and island containing all that they actually needed to survive. It was also said by Rosella that they became self-sufficient, learning to accomplish everything necessary for survival that they had once depended on the men for. This suggests that they did not, in the end, need men at all to thrive as a community, just as they did not require jewels or other material treasures.
dowry, or money or property given to husband at time of marriage

Sebastian reclaims his wife, after also proclaiming that Clarinda will be a good wife and that she will take on Rosella’s virtues. Jane O’Brien discusses the trajectory of a woman’s life in the period: Whether they’re mothers, ingenues or unruly woman, they are all women discovering how to find their way in the world. And it’s a pretty tough world. In a way, Clarinda must now, like her mother, find [her] way in the world, but in a form that is only granted to her by her father. So, while she may have freedom, she may also lack it, both in this scene and, presumably, throughout her life.

The dialogue in this speech implies there will be a double wedding (Clarinda marrying Raymond and Aminta marrying Albert), but no actual marriage ceremony occurs in the play. This is somewhat typical of seventeenth century comedies, where marriage is promised but not enacted. As a result, the play closes with a seemingly optimistic future, but one that has not yet come about, making the play’s ending more ambiguous.
